articles.title: How telecoms upgrade work sparked US flight chaos
articles.excerpt: US officials say the disruption was caused by old equipment overloading and not a cyber-attack.
articles.text: On Friday afternoon, a government contractor called L3Harris was continuing work on upgrading an aviation telecoms network. As it swapped out copper lines for fibre at a remote location in the US, L3Harris installed a router - a piece of equipment which basically directs traffic across the network. According to Duffy, that router started flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds. As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced "instability" on voice and ground communications, said Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). It took the aviation authority 45 minutes to identify where the problem was because maintenance is logged manually on paper. This meant the FAA had to "pore through" the physical documents "to figure out who's working on what", Bedford admitted. As a precaution as it tried to track down the cause, Bedford said the decision was made to ground all flights. Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned". He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper." Duffy said the system needed a complete overhaul, estimating a $50bn price tag. In the meantime, he said authorities would work to determine whether it was "incompetence" or faulty equipment that led to the outage. He also said there would be "re-evaluation" of allowing upgrades to be done during the day. In a statement on Saturday afternoon, L3Harris confirmed it was working with the FAA to modernise the airspace communications infrastructure and said it was supporting the agency with its investigation. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the firm said. Juliette Kayyem, US assistant secretary of Homeland Security under President Barack Obama, questioned why an upgrade was done on one of the week's busiest days for travel. "You don't do it on a Friday when there's lots of air traffic controllers," she said "You try to find ways to minimise its upgrade so you're not maybe doing it across the board in a single moment but you also have to have systems that are ready to step in if the upgrade in any way begins to threaten the system," Kayyem added. A spokesperson for L3Harris said is it "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel". He added: "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."
articles.summary: As it swapped out copper lines for fibre at a remote location in the US, L3Harris installed a router - a piece of equipment which basically directs traffic across the network. Juliette Kayyem, US assistant secretary of Homeland Security under President Barack Obama, questioned why an upgrade was done on one of the week's busiest days for travel. A spokesperson for L3Harris said is it "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel".

articles.title: Beware the New AI-Fueled Ransomware Boom
articles.excerpt: Fully automated ransomware hasn’t arrived—yet. But seemingly unsophisticated attackers are using AI tools to wreak havoc.
articles.text: With so much going on all the time, you may not have thought about ransomware and data extortion attacks in a minute, even though they’ve been among the the biggest cybersecurity threats to institutions—and, by extension, people—over the past decade. But in the new era of AI-powered and automated cyberattacks, the danger posed by ransomware is only increasing as cybercriminals profit by combining established methods with new techniques made possible or more accessible by AI. It is difficult to determine exact numbers of ransomware attacks, given that victims don’t always disclose incidents and attackers wildly inflate their claims. But researchers who specialize in tracking and attempting to de-duplicate the field agree that claimed incidents have spiked over the last few months. Some put the number of alleged ransomware attacks on leak sites—where groups post alleged victims—at nearly 3,000 attacks over the summer. This would mean a 20 to 40 percent increase since the spring by some estimates. And, crucially, researchers emphasize that while volume always fluctuates somewhat, ransomware attacks overall have been consistently and concerningly elevated in recent years. “What we see is most of the recent increase was fueled by international attacks; the United States was a little more steady, but still high, still a lot of attacks,” says Cynthia Kaiser, former FBI cyber deputy director who now leads research for the anti-ransomware platform Halcyon. “Internationally we’re seeing a lot more attacks. That to me is the really new part, and I do think it is in part fueled by AI.” Fully AI-powered ransomware attacks have yet to emerge, perhaps because the criminal business model already works so effectively. But cybercriminals do appear to be using LLMs for some of the more mundane aspects of their attacks. “We are seeing AI relied on more heavily in certain aspects of the ransomware attack chain, such as creating better phishing emails and in the negotiation process, but the ‘successful’ ransomware groups are still largely human operated,” says Allan Liska, a longtime ransomware researcher and threat intelligence analyst at Recorded Future. “But the fact that these groups are experimenting heavily with AI means that this could change going forward, and change quickly.” Kaiser notes that broader trends in scamming are always relevant to ransomware, because attackers often use the same types of phishing and social engineering techniques to gain initial access to targeted systems. In Japan, for example, successful scamming has spiked drastically in recent months as AI enables foreign attackers to generate consistently convincing content in Japanese for the first time.
articles.summary: But in the new era of AI-powered and automated cyberattacks, the danger posed by ransomware is only increasing as cybercriminals profit by combining established methods with new techniques made possible or more accessible by AI. Kaiser notes that broader trends in scamming are always relevant to ransomware, because attackers often use the same types of phishing and social engineering techniques to gain initial access to targeted systems. In Japan, for example, successful scamming has spiked drastically in recent months as AI enables foreign attackers to generate consistently convincing content in Japanese for the first time.

articles.title: Uber confirms hackers stole thousands of drivers’ license information in data breach
articles.excerpt: The ridesharing giant said drivers' license information stored by AI cloud company Fireworks AI was stolen during a security incident.
articles.text: Uber is notifying thousands of drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers. In notices filed this week with several U.S. attorneys general, including California, the ride-hail giant said it was notified on October 9 by the provider that hackers broke in and stole internal credentials, which were used to access Uber’s data. The company said it subsequently began notifying affected drivers that their personal information was stored with the provider. TechCrunch has learned that the provider is Fireworks AI, which lets developers access and use open AI models. Fireworks reported a data breach last month in which hackers stole its customers’ information, including billing data and some private AI datasets. Online productivity startup Notion confirmed its data was also stolen in the Fireworks hack. “The notices to drivers are in relation to a security incident impacting one of our third-party vendors, Fireworks.ai, which had access to some Uber data,” an Uber spokesperson told TechCrunch, deferring our questions to Fireworks. Uber did not say how many customers are affected by the breach, nor how many drivers it was notifying about the incident. When reached by email, a spokesperson for Fireworks confirmed that the company identified a security issue involving unauthorized access to some of its systems, which affected customer data, but the spokesperson did not address our questions about the incident. According to data breach notices seen by TechCrunch, the stolen data includes driver’s licenses of 2,567 individuals in Massachusetts, 3,430 people across South Carolina, and 1,873 residents of Rhode Island. A filing with Illinois showed that some state residents had their driver’s license information stolen, but that the number of affected people was pending. Uber also notified drivers who live in California, but did not say how many had their information stolen. The number is expected to rise as more data breach notifications roll in. Fireworks attributed its breach to a financially motivated cybercriminal group whose goals are to sell stolen tokens for accessing large language models, or LLMs. No known cybercriminal group has taken credit for the data theft. This is Uber’s second known data breach this year. The company reported a security incident at its Uber Freight truck shipping unit, for which an extortion gang took credit for stealing data. Updated with a response from Fireworks.
articles.summary: In notices filed this week with several U.S. attorneys general, including California, the ride-hail giant said it was notified on October 9 by the provider that hackers broke in and stole internal credentials, which were used to access Uber’s data. Fireworks attributed its breach to a financially motivated cybercriminal group whose goals are to sell stolen tokens for accessing large language models, or LLMs. The company reported a security incident at its Uber Freight truck shipping unit, for which an extortion gang took credit for stealing data.

articles.title: This week in science: PTSD prediction, phishing while tired, an exoplanet
articles.excerpt: The regular news roundup with NPR's science podcast Short Wave covers a possible use for AI in emergency rooms, a distant planet and the link between cybersecurity and Daylight Saving Time.
articles.text: This week in science: PTSD prediction, phishing while tired, an exoplanet The regular news roundup with NPR's science podcast Short Wave covers a possible use for AI in emergency rooms, a distant planet and the link between cybersecurity and Daylight Saving Time. It's time now for our science news roundup from Short Wave, NPR's science podcast. I am joined by the show's hosts, Emily Kwong and Regina Barber. Hello to both of you. REGINA BARBER, BYLINE: Hey. EMILY KWONG, BYLINE: Hey. DETROW: You were in stereo just now. DETROW: It was great. BARBER: We planned that. DETROW: So you've brought us three science stories that caught your attention. What are they? KWONG: How AI can help emergency room workers identify patients who may develop PTSD. BARBER: A new technique that helps us find really faint planets beyond our solar system. DETROW: You know how I feel about space. BARBER: That's right. KWONG: We put it in there for you. BARBER: That's why I picked it. KWONG: (Inaudible) put this story in there for you (laughter). KWONG: And why daylight saving time could be bad for cybersecurity. DETROW: All right. Let's start with - this is interesting. There's been so many stories about AI identifying healthcare trends that might be hard for doctors to spot. Let's talk about this. Identifying... DETROW: ...PTSD in emergency departments. KWONG: This is very interesting. So researchers took trauma patients answers' to a routine screening question - what brought you to the emergency department today? They fed the answers to that question into an AI model that was designed to predict the patient's risk of developing PTSD a month later. DETROW: Huh. I mean, how good was the model making that prediction? BARBER: So it got it right around 95% of the cases. A psychologist and lead researcher, Katharina Schultebraucks, says that these results are exciting because they're using a patient's story in their own words. KATHARINA SCHULTEBRAUCKS: Some people talk, like, very elaborative of what happens. Some are in such high distress they may only say a few words and a few sentences. And we are looking not on PTSD symptoms right now, but we're looking in what happens in the future. BARBER: They published their findings in the journal Nature Communications. DETROW: I'm curious, is this something that clinicians have been missing? KWONG: Yeah, so when trained clinicians are screening for PTSD risk, they do tend to find it. The problem is that giving a PTSD risk assessment is an extra step that a lot of emergency departments just simply do not have time for. You know, they're, like, tending to the emergency. There's also the stigma around mental health that might clam up some patients. So using this model could streamline the process, and medical professionals can act sooner to prevent PTSD from developing. BARBER: And Scott, what's unique about this work is that the model gave its reasoning at each step of the analysis. MUNMUN DE CHOUDHURY: What this work does, it says that the AI doesn't have to be a black box. BARBER: So this is Munmun De Choudhury, a computer scientist not involved in the work. She said this work has real potential to guide clinicians to the right kind of interventions. DETROW: Perpetual question with this stuff - are there worries about privacy of sending a patient's words to an AI model? KWONG: Good question. Katharina says that the model did not share the data on a cloud service and was HIPAA-compliant. But she adds that it is important any patient consents to having their information recorded and used by an AI model. DETROW: So new topic. BARBER: (Laughter) Yeah. DETROW: New exoplanet. Let's - this is a - meaning a planet beyond our solar system. DETROW: What is this technique that scientists used to find it? BARBER: So this exoplanet was actually already known. A team of researchers studied existing images of the star it orbits to see if light from 51 Eridani b could be found, just to kind of verify this technique. And this is important because often it's hard to see exoplanets in images. KWONG: And that's because the light that exoplanets reflect from the closest star is often much fainter than the light the star gives off. KWONG: So the star, like, kind of hides the planet. DETROW: I mean, so how did they uncover it, then? Because again, stars, very bright. DETROW: Planets, when they're far away, not very bright. BARBER: So they subtracted light from the image until they could clearly see the planet and not the stars. The paper was published in Nature last week. And this new technique corrects that issue and corrects for millions of more issues that can make it harder to find an exoplanet, like the telescope being unstable or instrumental errors or temperature fluctuations. DETROW: Is this kind of like in a - in, like, a cops TV show where they're looking at the security camera and they say, oh, enhance on that one image, and they zoom in? BARBER: I mean, kind of (laughter). But Scott, what I'm actually surprised about is that they did all of this with just physics knowledge and algorithms and no AI. DETROW: So what can these images tell us about this planet? KWONG: So yeah, because these images were taken in infrared by the powerful James Webb Space Telescope, they can tell us more about what these exoplanets are made out of. RODRIGO FERRER-CHAVEZ: With this, it is the first time that we can actually get this specific information-rich image of this planet that might tell us a lot about how it formed. KWONG: That's lead author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, a Ph.D. candidate at Northwestern University. He also says that this tool can be used to find even more exoplanets hiding out in James Webb Space Telescope images. BARBER: This technique can also be used to make future telescopes, that are already supposed to be more powerful, even better at finding exoplanets. But I do want to say that other astronomers I talked to said that this is just one cool technique of many that scientists are developing for future research in finding these faint, distant worlds. DETROW: OK. All right, back here on Earth. Third story. It's about sleep. KWONG: And daylight saving. BARBER: Yeah. So, Scott, did you know that nearly one-third of U.S. adults don't get enough sleep? DETROW: Honestly, I would assume the number is higher. BARBER: (Laughter) Yeah. DETROW: One-third actually sounds promising (laughter). BARBER: And we know that it's bad for our health, right? It's bad for decision-making. KWONG: But just how bad is it for decision-making if you lose a modest amount of sleep? That's what Eitan Schechtman, an assistant professor at the University of California, Irvine wanted to know. And he found a fun way to test this with phishing attacks. KWONG: His university regularly sends fake phishing emails to staff to train them on cybersecurity. These emails contain suspicious links you are not supposed to click. But would they click if they were a little sleepy? DETROW: Interesting. Did this become a full experiment? BARBER: Yeah, so Eitan worked with the university's security team to divide 11,000 participants into two groups. Some people got the fishing email the Monday before daylight saving, and some got it the Monday immediately after, you know, when we can assume some may have lost an hour of sleep. So people emailed after daylight saving were 13% more likely to fall for the phishing attack the following morning and click that bad link. The study was published in the Proceedings of National Academy of Sciences this week. KWONG: I spoke to Muhammad Adeel Rishi, a sleep specialist at Indiana University School of Medicine who wasn't involved in this study. He found the finding compelling and said it adds to growing evidence about the consequences of daylight saving. Spring forward has been linked to an increase in heart attacks and fatal traffic accidents. DETROW: And apparently cybersecurity problems. What's the solution here? BARBER: So Eitan wants cybersecurity companies to be aware of this finding so they can beef up their security for any moments where there's widespread sleep loss. So think about holidays or major sporting events. EITAN SCHECHTMAN: There might be more of these - more susceptibility to click these links or generally to make impulsive decisions, whether it's on the road, in the stock market or cybersecurity-related decision. DETROW: Some places have just, like, gotten rid of time changes, right? DETROW: Like most of Arizona and Hawaii. KWONG: Yes. This is a whole other debate. But just to put science's finger on the scale, multiple studies have shown that standard time is healthier for our bodies. Standard time has more natural light in the morning, which better aligns to our bodies' circadian rhythms. DETROW: All right. Good thing we're in standard time right now. BARBER: That's right. DETROW: That is Emily Kwong and Regina Barber with NPR's science podcast Short Wave, where you can listen for new discoveries and the science behind the headlines. Thanks to both of you. BARBER: Thank you, Scott. (SOUNDBITE OF PHARRELL WILLIAMS SONG, "NUMBER ONE (FEAT. KANYE WEST)") Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. articles.summary: A team of researchers studied existing images of the star it orbits to see if light from 51 Eridani b could be found, just to kind of verify this technique. But I do want to say that other astronomers I talked to said that this is just one cool technique of many that scientists are developing for future research in finding these faint, distant worlds. KWONG: I spoke to Muhammad Adeel Rishi, a sleep specialist at Indiana University School of Medicine who wasn't involved in this study.

articles.title: United Airlines blocks AI agents from booking flights, citing cybersecurity risks
articles.excerpt: The airline said it will not allow customers to use AI agents to book flights and manage reservations.
articles.text: United Airlines said it will restrict access to AI agents seeking to book flights and manage reservations on their users’ behalf, citing a risk to cybersecurity and undermining federal regulations. The airline is the latest American corporate giant to prevent customers from using AI agents and autonomous assistants to access their systems. The move comes as airlines and banks are struggling to differentiate between real customers and AI systems operating on their behalf, such as when users share their logins with their AI assistants. Sharing passwords with apps and assistants can create security risks if those credentials get leaked or exposed. United warns that “sharing account credentials with personal, third-party, AI assistants can expose sensitive information, and actions taken by these tools may result in unintended purchases, account changes, or use of MileagePlus miles.” The airline also warns of a risk of violating federal aviation rules, such as requiring that a human completes flight check-ins to acknowledge that their bags do not contain banned substances. “As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants,” the airline said in a statement. “This work includes updates to our booking, ticketing and distribution policies.” The airline’s move follows a warning from banks, including Bank of America, which last week urged customers not to share their passwords with their AI assistants.
articles.summary: United Airlines said it will restrict access to AI agents seeking to book flights and manage reservations on their users’ behalf, citing a risk to cybersecurity and undermining federal regulations. The airline also warns of a risk of violating federal aviation rules, such as requiring that a human completes flight check-ins to acknowledge that their bags do not contain banned substances. “As a result, United is taking steps to restrict access — directly within our digital platforms and indirectly via travel agencies and aggregators — to prohibit use by unauthorized, third-party personal AI agents or assistants,” the airline said in a statement.
